scopeNote: This assessment expands the previous product-only scope to include secure, reliable production operation. The lower total reflects the wider goal, not a measured regression in reverse-engineering features.
assessmentNote: Quality run [40247230850](https://github.com/xdCloudy/REAmon/actions/runs/40247230850) passed the full Docker unit gate and production-stack acceptance on commit `baa5634a`; local and LAN readiness endpoints returned ready with database and artifact checks ok, at that checkpoint, deployment revision verification had not yet been performed. On 2026-10-26, kali_shell, execute_code, proxy_brain, and execute_playwright gained verified signed project scope, user/mount/PID namespaces, project-only workspaces, and per-project /tmp scratch. /var/tmp, /dev/shm, and /opt/output remain per-run private mounts. Generated files are canonicalized under project scratch and moved to a unique project tool-outputs path without a second full-size copy. The project root is read-only to the sandbox UID; only scratch and tool-outputs are writable. Focused Docker suites passed 46 MCP execution/capture/Playwright tests plus 5 subtests and 15 agent identity/generated-file tests. Live Kali smokes verified read-only project roots, writable project scratch and tool-outputs, canonical same-mount generated-file transfer, compiled C output, and sibling workspace/scratch/process isolation. The rebuilt active Kali image launches Chromium version 156.0.8078.4. Terminal shells retain ticket-derived project scope and cleanup behavior. Legacy graph routes reject scanner-only auth and the agent rejects identical master and scanner keys. Broker-managed workers now route kali_shell, execute_code, execute_playwright, and proxy_brain through signed-scope verification, a four-container admission cap, project-only mounts, resource limits, capped output, and per-run cleanup. Thirteen focused broker worker tests and 14 MCP execution tests pass in Docker; the 27-case capture-routing suite also passes. A live Docker Engine smoke verified read-only workspace, writable project scratch, separate stdout/stderr, and worker/network cleanup. The rebuilt local agent, Kali, and broker containers are healthy. A valid agent-signed kali_shell request completed through the broker and disposable worker with exit code 0; worker container and network cleanup were confirmed. Chromium launched in the active Kali container at version 156.0.8078.4. At that checkpoint, terminal execution, worker storage quotas, scoped broker ownership, egress policy, generated-file transfer, and upgrade/backup/restore validation remained open. This weighted estimate is evidence-backed progress, not release certification. The active Kali execution wrapper now applies RLIMIT_NOFILE=256 and RLIMIT_CORE=0 through util-linux prlimit to each arbitrary-code child; focused Docker coverage and a live-image probe verified both limits. This does not replace the remaining worker-level CPU, memory, disk, and lifetime controls. The interactive terminal now inherits the same `RLIMIT_NOFILE=256` and `RLIMIT_CORE=0` through its PTY launcher; the focused terminal plus arbitrary-execution Docker suites pass. The interactive terminal now enters a private PID namespace as well as user and mount namespaces. Docker unit coverage passes (7 tests plus 4 subtests), and a live Kali smoke confirmed the shell is PID 1 with only itself and `ps` visible in `/proc`. The Docker broker now fails closed when the configured active broker-container cap cannot be verified; focused Docker broker plumbing, ownership, and policy suites pass 88 checks, including proof that an unverified count denies creation without contacting Docker. The rebuilt active Kali image passes `pip check` with no broken requirements; legacy GraphQL-Cop, SSTImap, and AD dependencies are isolated from the MCP runtime, and their commands passed live startup smokes. On 2026-10-26 the Docker broker added fail-closed per-project worker admission (default two active workers per project, within the global four-worker cap), keyed by a SHA-256 project label so Docker metadata does not expose project IDs. The active broker reports healthy with limits 4/2. Docker regression suites pass 16 project-worker tests, 13 ownership checks, 18 plumbing checks, and 57 policy checks; Compose configuration validates. This improves fairness and bounds concurrent work per project; it does not replace multi-replica admission coordination or storage, egress, and lifetime quotas. The broker ownership boundary was tightened on 2026-10-26: disposable project workers no longer carry the generic broker-owned label, and the generic Docker proxy rejects operations on any legacy dual-labeled project worker. The shared host admission lock now serializes generic tool-container and project-worker creates; its count fails closed and sums separate generic and project-worker labels. Docker suites pass 18 worker tests, 17 ownership checks, 21 plumbing checks, and 57 policy checks. The active broker is healthy with a 48-container host cap and worker limits 4/2. A live agent-signed broker dispatch returned exit code 0 and left zero active project workers. The generic Docker broker now also denies network discovery/lifecycle APIs plus `/events` and `/system/df`, and rejects attempts to join names in the private project-worker network namespace. Docker broker suites pass 19 worker tests, 17 ownership checks, 30 plumbing checks, and 58 policy checks. The rebuilt active broker is healthy; a live signed `kali_shell` dispatch returned exit code 0 and left zero active workers and no residual capacity count. On 2026-10-26, Metasploit session registrations now retain project/user ownership metadata; project session list, interact, and kill routes verify strict project ownership at the webapp and sidecar boundaries, and unowned legacy sessions are hidden. The project-switching UI clears prior session data before displaying another project. Validation: 19 isolated Docker Python cases, 10 focused webapp cases, TypeScript type-check, and Python compilation passed. Docker Compose service-level rebuild and LAN verification remain outstanding; session ownership is process-local because the Metasploit console restart terminates its live sessions, and jobs remain admin-only. In persistent mode the agent now refuses startup if PostgreSQL checkpoint initialization is unavailable, closes any partial pool, and does not silently switch to volatile MemorySaver; explicitly disabled mode retains the in-memory option. Four isolated Docker startup and shutdown tests pass, including checkpoint-pool cleanup. Live deployment recovery across an agent restart remains to be exercised. A live PostgreSQL probe wrote a unique checkpoint, closed its first connection pool, recovered the state through a new pool, and deleted the probe thread; full agent restart recovery remains to be exercised. On 2026-10-26 the interactive terminal proxy gained a broker-backed, ticket-derived per-session PTY worker path. The agent signs a short-lived context, the broker re-verifies user/project/session and graph scope, applies host/global/per-project admission, and creates a resource-capped worker with project-only mounts and disconnect cleanup. Source compilation and whitespace validation pass. The focused Docker integration suites and a broker-level Docker Engine PTY smoke have since passed; the smoke executed a shell command, returned output, and confirmed worker/network cleanup. It patched the scope verifier, so actual agent-ticket-to-broker/browser flow, resize and graph-call acceptance, and LAN deployment remain pending. On 2026-10-26, the normal Compose/install path now builds the dedicated REAmon language worker and starts the filtered broker. Compose validation passed with default and optional profiles, focused broker tests passed (30), and a constrained no-network image smoke passed for Python, C, Java, Go, Node/TypeScript, Ruby, Perl, Rust, and .NET SDK 10.0.402 as UID/GID 65534 with read-only root and dropped capabilities. The worker home/cache path is writable through project-scoped /tmp. Lifecycle shell regressions passed (22 status assertions and 13 update-map assertions). Browser-to-agent-to-broker and LAN execution, multi-replica admission, storage/egress/lifetime quotas, and restart/cancellation recovery remain open; no live services were restarted. The install/update worker-profile regression was tightened on 2026-10-26; the focused build lifecycle suite now passes 81 assertions, including explicit checks that both install and source-driven rebuilds activate the project-worker profile. A new versioned Lua 5.4 reconstruction fixture passes inside an unprivileged, no-network Docker container: stripped bytecode decompiles, the output passes luac5.4 -p, and original/reconstructed runtime output matches. The fixture includes nested local functions, a branch, and a loop; it does not establish broad Lua version or semantic coverage. On 2026-10-26, a no-database isolated Rust DEX-to-Java run completed the 65,195-class Cross Stitch Joy APK in 4,998 seconds, producing 65,190 Java files; the response correctly warned that only 500 files and 10,000 methods were returned. The class-isolated strategy recovered from 16 OOM kills and used simple fallback output for some complex classes, but pathological attempts reached the 4 GiB cap. Database persistence, UI retrieval of capped output, and fidelity comparison remain unverified. The Compose default for the Rust DEX analyzer now matches the 80,000-unit analyzer limit and the 100,000-code-unit ingestion bound, replacing the 500-unit production default. Focused analyzer Docker tests pass (12), and Compose configuration validates; a full-output isolated run is checking materialization and response size before this capability is counted as completed. On 2026-10-26, the completed 80,000-unit-cap DEX QA run superseded the earlier 500-unit checkpoint: 6,924 seconds, 65,190 Java units returned and copied to derived storage (183,388,129 bytes) from 65,195 discovered classes. The 10,000-method evidence cap remains. Failed-class descriptor lookup is implemented and passed a real QA DEX lookup; project database ingestion and visualizer access remain open. The DEX method evidence path now preserves discovered and returned counts, truncation state, and indexed method totals in visualizer diagnostics; 59 focused provider, task-executor, route, and UI tests pass, and the webapp type-check and ESLint pass. The QA project referenced in prior work was not present in the current local database, so live ingestion remains unverified. The LAN webapp was rebuilt from the pushed DEX method coverage change and now reports revision a3ce570c with a matching image label; localhost and LAN readiness both report database and artifact checks ok. The bounded DEX method paging and streamed persistence path is now implemented. Rust and Python tests pass in Docker; real APK runs streamed all 416,783 methods on the large structured pass and all 33,401 methods on the small full analyzer/server path, with bounded page cleanup verified. Webapp task-executor tests pass (13) and Prisma type-check passes after generating the client from this checkout. Run-scoped pending rows are promoted atomically only after task success. The current QA has not exercised a real database-backed project task or AI retrieval, and calls/references remain capped. Retry recovery also clears orphaned run-scoped pending method rows for the same task before the new run writes its first batch; the focused task-executor test and type-check pass. Revalidated the pinned DEX Unicode patch through a full real-APK analyzer/server run: 11,939 of 11,939 classes and 33,401 of 33,401 methods returned, with zero character-boundary panics and zero class fallbacks. The comparison used the patched isolated analyzer image and read-only stored APK volume; no project database rows were changed. The disposable PostgreSQL integration test exercises task leasing, streamed batch ingestion, atomic promotion, and the actual MCP code-unit listing. It initially found that a negated JSON-path predicate hid observations without the pending key; replacing that predicate with a persisted is_pending boolean fixed retrieval. The integration and 45 focused webapp tests pass, and type-check passes. The analyzer was mocked in the database integration test; current-provider execution and AI explanation/rewrite context against the QA project remain to be verified. On 2026-10-26, a real Cross Stitch Joy APK completed through the current Rust DEX provider and database task path: 11,176 function observations, 1,560 symbols, 4,000 call edges, and 4,000 field/string references were persisted, pending observations reached zero, and MCP code/relationship lookups returned stored results. The run took 405 seconds. Focused PostgreSQL integration independently verifies atomic promotion; AI-context retrieval and fidelity remain unverified. The visualizer run diagnostics now show provider-returned call and field/string counts and explicitly flag truncated relationship evidence. Focused API/component suites pass 44 tests, scoped ESLint passes, and the changed visualizer files have no TypeScript diagnostics; unrelated existing test fixtures still fail the full repository type-check. The AI explanation route now retrieves call edges and field/string references by the selected function stable key, constrained to that same project, artifact, analysis run, and provider; labels are normalized before model use. Its focused route suite passes 14 tests and scoped ESLint passes. DEX member rewrites now resolve the selected class method to its stored function observation keys before fetching direct call edges, so large run-wide edge prefixes cannot hide the selected method neighbors. A focused regression confirms same-run direct-callee source reaches rewrite context; the 15-test explanation/rewrite route suite passes and scoped ESLint passes. On 2026-10-26, the LAN webapp and agent were rebuilt and report healthy with source revision 546d9be7. The agent image uses local build-revision metadata; the current WebSocket and Metasploit ownership source changes have not yet been deployed. On 2026-10-26, the visualizer gained a project/run-level AI function queue: it scans at most 40 source-linked units from four pages, queues up to 10 eligible functions round-robin across files, persists attempt status in the existing database, supports batch cancellation, and links each result to its source file. Cross-file results are not merged or auto-accepted. Browser/database acceptance and multi-file fixture validation remain pending. The LAN webapp was rebuilt from commit `b4cddfe9`; production TypeScript compilation and bundling passed, the image label matches the commit, and container health plus `/api/health` report healthy. The agent remains on `546d9be7`, so agent-side job registration and Metasploit job-ownership deployment remain open. At the initial queue rollout checkpoint, the LAN webapp image was b4cddfe9 and the agent was f5f95599; the Metasploit sidecar was force-recreated to load project-scoped job ownership. Current LAN snapshot on 2026-10-26: webapp and agent were rebuilt from main revision 4b91518e and both are healthy; localhost /api/health returns status=ok; Kali remains healthy. Isolated Docker checks pass for C/C++ compiler validation (8 tests), agent REST auth (10 tests and 20 subtests), graph auth (1 test), project-session scope (2 tests), Metasploit HTTP/job ownership (24 tests and 11 subtests), and webapp session ownership (8 tests). Live owner/non-owner session/job acceptance and backup/restore remain open. The authenticated live agent validator at revision 4b91518e also accepted and rejected synthetic C and C++ sources as expected; each response contained the exact SHA-256 of the submitted source. On 2026-10-26, kali_shell, execute_code, proxy_brain, and execute_playwright were made asynchronous end-to-end at the MCP boundary. Their cancellable broker client closes its TCP connection when the agent task is cancelled; the broker treats disconnect as a cancellation signal and removes the disposable worker. The focused MCP execution/capture Docker suite passed 51 tests and the broker worker Docker suite passed 42 tests, including socket cancellation and Docker Desktop bind-path coverage. Live deployment revealed and fixed three worker-launch mismatches: the broker and agent had different workspace mounts, the pentest worker tag did not match the built Kali image, and nested Docker Desktop bind mounts needed the daemon host path instead of its temporary WSL shim path. After rebuilding/recreating the broker and restarting Kali with no active sessions, jobs, or workers, a valid agent-signed direct call to the deployed async kali_shell function started a real sleep worker. Cancelling its task propagated through the broker socket; the worker container and network were removed, and the temporary project workspace was cleaned. FastMCP 3.2.4 registered all four tools as async. Agent MCP ainvoke and browser-level cancellation acceptance remain open. On 2026-10-26, live deployment wiring was corrected so the agent and broker resolve the same host workspace, the broker uses the built Kali worker image, and Windows workspace binds are translated for Docker Desktop. The agent image was rebuilt and reports healthy; 31 API cancellation tests passed against that deployed image, and the broker worker/policy/ownership/plumbing suite passes 42 tests. A signed live kali_shell call through the deployed async tool function launched a disposable worker; cancellation propagated through the broker socket and removed its worker and network. Agent MCP ainvoke cancellation now sends the MCP notifications/cancelled message. A live authenticated /kali/exec start/cancel smoke removed the disposable worker and its network. Browser UI cancellation remains unverified. The weighted score stays 63.7% because worker quotas, multi-replica admission, capacity review, multi-user acceptance, and backup/restore gates remain. On the rebuilt local agent, live GET requests to /workspace/jobs and /sessions returned 200 with the configured master key and 401 with scanner-only or missing credentials; the sessions proxy reached the authenticated Kali session sidecar. LAN owner/non-owner acceptance remains open.

workstreams.name: Core analysis and visualizer workflow
workstreams.summary: Imports, provider execution, database-backed code units, source navigation, and a multi-provider visualizer are established across several language and binary workflows. A worker-run SLB2 inspection of the 1.26 GB PS5 QA artifact completed and persisted two bounded container facts. The 65,195-class QA APK completed all 10 DEX files in an isolated run in 6,924 seconds: 65,190 Java units were returned and all 65,190 were copied to derived storage (183,388,129 bytes). The 80,000-unit response cap did not truncate class output; five classes remained unreconstructed, and method evidence remains capped at 10,000. Failed classes now retain bounded DEX/index/descriptor/reason evidence, with a bounded descriptor-only lookup for timeout and memory-killed classes; a real QA APK class lookup passed. On 2026-10-26, the DEX provider emitted stable artifact-scoped facts for failed classes, and the visualizer presents up to 100 validated identities with reasons. The DEX provider now retains discovered and returned method counts and truncation status; task settlement persists class, method, and failure observations; and the visualizer separately shows discovered, returned, and database-indexed method counts. Focused provider, task-executor, API, and component checks pass (59), with TypeScript and ESLint clean. The live QA project has two older completed runs that stored only 500 of 65,195 class identities and no method rows; a fresh run is still needed to verify current database ingestion and AI retrieval. The pinned Rust DEX decompiler Unicode cast-parser panic is fixed with UTF-8 byte indexing, covered by a Rust regression test, and deployed in the healthy LAN analyzer. The Java DEX class path now defaults to bounded batches of 8, with existing adaptive split retries for timeout, memory, and panic failures; focused Docker analyzer tests pass (14), and the LAN analyzer is healthy with batch size 8. A fresh analyzer-level QA probe completed all 10 DEX files in 4,835 seconds with batch size 8, returning 65,190 Java files; the prior one-class run took 6,924 seconds. Returned source bytes differed by 147,100, so file-level output parity remains unverified. A standalone structured pass counted 416,783 implemented DEX methods while returning 10,000; at that checkpoint, call and reference output each stopped at 4,000. The Rust prepass now counts all implemented methods before applying the response cap, and the rebuilt analyzer is healthy. The QA probe bypassed the webapp task persistence path; database ingestion and AI retrieval remain unverified. The coverage inventory now reconciles discoveredMethodCount, returnedMethodCount, and indexed function observations for newly executed DEX tasks. The Rust structured DEX pass now writes bounded 1,000-method pages; the analyzer streams them as NDJSON, and the DEX provider stages observations in run-scoped batches before atomic promotion on success. Docker QA against the stored 6.79 MB APK discovered and streamed all 33,401 methods across 34 pages, reported no method truncation, and removed temporary pages. A separate full structured pass against the larger APK returned all 416,783 methods across 417 pages. Task-executor tests cover pending-source promotion and type-check passes after regenerating Prisma from this checkout. This verifies analyzer transport and source-level persistence logic, not a real project task or AI retrieval. Rust DEX analysis now writes call and reference spill pages of 1,000 rows, bounded to 4,200 pages per evidence type and 256 MiB combined. The Python analyzer validates page names and counts before NDJSON delivery and removes temporary pages; the webapp validates and persists call edges plus field/string references in run-scoped batches. The analyzer image builds; 15 focused Docker analyzer tests, 5 provider tests, and a clean package-lock-based webapp type-check pass. The full QA APK task through the current provider, database, MCP, and AI context remains unverified. The opt-in PostgreSQL executor integration now streams functions, symbols, call edges, and field references, verifies successful atomic promotion, and reads completed relationships through MCP; no pending observations remain. The provider is mocked in this fixture, so the real QA project task and AI-context retrieval remain open. On 2026-10-26, the current Rust DEX provider completed a real Cross Stitch Joy APK project task in 405 seconds and promoted 11,176 functions, 1,560 symbols, 4,000 calls, and 4,000 references with no pending observations; MCP code and relationship queries retrieved stored results. Discovered/returned/indexed function coverage now reconciles streamed observations. The visualizer run diagnostics now show provider-returned call and field/string counts and explicitly flag truncated relationship evidence; the focused API and component suites pass 44 tests. The project function agent queue now scans a bounded selection from a completed run, queues per-file rewrites, stores batch state, supports cancellation, and links each result back to its source file. The deployed webapp build and health endpoint pass; interactive database/browser acceptance remains open.
workstreams.remaining: Verify real-run DEX evidence in AI explanation and rewrite context; compare reconstructed output with bytecode; exercise relationship-cap truncation and page cleanup on larger workloads. Complete authenticated browser/database acceptance and multi-file fixture validation for the project queue.
workstreams.basis: Imports, provider execution, stored code units, source navigation, and review workflows exist. The profiler recognizes structurally plausible PyInstaller CArchive cookies in native executables and records package/runtime metadata. A pinned, MIT-licensed pyinstxtractor-go snapshot now runs in a bounded isolated service, extracts capped Python bytecode children, persists each accepted child as a task-scoped derived artifact and database code unit, and feeds up to four not-yet-decompiled modules per run to pycdc while skipping exact-hash modules already completed in prior project runs; child records retain executable, archive-path, extractor-revision, bytecode-hash, and recovered-source provenance. The Go image builds and webapp type-checks; representative archive execution and fidelity validation remain open. The Python bytecode workflow pairs hash-verified recovered source with bounded bytecode in the visualizer and MCP dossier, keeps module-wide evidence out of selected-function context, and carries the raw bytecode magic without inferring a runtime version. Native Mach-O analysis stores exact-address Swift/Objective-C metadata and exposes capped, hash-checked ReIPA pseudocode alternatives; the visualizer can compare native provider outputs by canonical function identity across differing saved paths and output-language labels. Isolated pinned Glaurung, Kuna, and Fission providers persist bounded native C-like pseudocode; Fission's exact-hash per-function outputs are included as same-function AI context only after binary-hash, identity, completed-run, and output-hash checks. Kuna also stores assembly, selected call/jump/reference edges, and bounded opcode sequences. A pinned isolated Recurse MCP adapter stores bounded per-function VTIL-style lift evidence and optimizer counters, displayed with its semantic limits; container build, runtime, and fixture comparison remain open. The visualizer and rewrite context compare Ghidra/Kuna instruction sequences across providers only when normalized architecture groups agree, exclude same-function cross-provider self-matches, and keep provider, analysis-run, artifact-hash, identity, and similarity provenance with reused names. Kuna's v1.878 analyzer image and end-to-end worker have been exercised against a system ELF binary. A read-only Ghidra p-code emulator also persists bounded, confidence-labeled control-flow-flattening transitions as visualizer navigation evidence. Ghidra now offers separate opt-in pinned BcfClean and CffDeflatten passes with bounded scans, emulation audits, and hash-checked alternatives in the visualizer and rewrite context; runtime and representative fixture comparisons remain open. The new Fission adapter still needs image-build, runtime, and fixture comparison. Newly settled decompile/disassemble tasks now persist a centralized coverage inventory after database ingestion, separating provider-discovered, provider-returned, raw-observed, and indexed units, along with the unreturned remainder, not-observed and not-indexed counts, explicit WebAssembly invalid/excess record omissions, unvisited functions when discovered and visited counts exist, truncation, and classifications the provider reported. The visualizer uses the stored inventory, shows not-visited units only when discovered and visited counts exist, and labels older runs without it. TypeScript type-check and targeted ESLint pass; provider coverage and runtime behavior remain to be exercised, and unsupported/skip/exclusion classifications remain unknown when engines do not report them. The pinned univdreams analyzer stores a bounded `.ud` module view, compile-back binary, exact hashes, provider revision, and byte-identity result; the selected-unit visualizer reports that result with its limits. A generated 34-byte WASM module, a small synthetic static ELF, an optimized dynamic ELF, and a debug dynamic ELF completed the isolated runtime smoke with byte-identical compile-back. A narrow REAmon-owned univdreams backport clamps non-PLT ranges at named PLT boundaries; maintained-source validation also compiled and persisted the debug ELF with a verified output hash. These synthetic cases do not establish broad format coverage or behavioral fidelity. A separate pinned Miasm provider now lifts executable-section symbol/entry-point candidates in PE/ELF to bounded simplified IR, stores hash-attributed per-function artifacts and block-count changes, and makes exact same-function evidence available to rewrite and MCP context only after identity, run, input-hash, and output-hash checks; x86-64 and AArch64 ELF plus two-function synthetic PE DLL export API smokes pass; other architectures and fixture comparisons remain open. The worker registry now receives an independent 30-second process heartbeat during synchronous analyzer runs, and graph projection is queued outside the analysis polling loop; runtime validation of this revision remains pending. A bounded SLB2 inspector is wired to stored artifact profiles; the real QA PUP table shape and 1.26 GB declared size match the stored artifact, and production build and provider registration passed; a worker-run task against the real 1.26 GB QA PUP completed and persisted two accepted facts plus analysis evidence without decryption. Broader firmware and language fixtures remain open. A focused DEX diagnostics improvement now converts bounded failed-class identities into stable artifact-scoped database facts and exposes up to 100 validated entries with reasons in the visualizer. The provider/API/component checks pass (44), and TypeScript plus ESLint pass; database persistence, AI retrieval, and deployed UI delivery remain open. On 2026-10-26, the visualizer gained a project/run-level AI function queue: it scans at most 40 source-linked units from four pages, queues up to 10 eligible functions round-robin across files, persists attempt status in the existing database, supports batch cancellation, and links each result to its source file. Cross-file results are not merged or auto-accepted. Browser/database acceptance and multi-file fixture validation remain pending. The LAN webapp was rebuilt from commit `b4cddfe9`; production TypeScript compilation and bundling passed, the image label matches the commit, and container health plus `/api/health` report healthy. The agent remains on `546d9be7`, so agent-side job registration and Metasploit job-ownership deployment remain open.

workstreams.name: Database-grounded project memory and provenance
workstreams.summary: Project observations, symbols, relationships, source drafts, review receipts, hashes, provider versions, and run evidence ground AI context and cross-provider name reuse. Analyst-reviewed cross-artifact function matches now persist exact pair evidence and supply bounded naming context to explanations and rewrites for exact matched functions, with duplicate pair records resolved by their latest analyst review. Their matcher includes a separately stored, low-weight exact string-reference overlap when both providers supply complete lists. A bounded REA Evidence v2 bundle importer validates canonical identities and manifests, stores complete provider-attributed records idempotently, links only exact artifact hashes, and supplies a bounded untrusted subset to rewrite context. An opt-in PostgreSQL integration test now creates an isolated project, artifact, and DEX task; executes the real task-executor transaction with a streamed function batch; verifies success-only promotion clears the pending flag; and retrieves both functions through the actual MCP code-unit listing. The isolated run exposed and fixed a PostgreSQL JSON-null filter that had hidden ordinary observations when the pending attribute was absent. The provider itself is mocked in this integration test, so analyzer-to-database behavior on a real project artifact remains open. The PostgreSQL integration fixture now confirms streamed function, symbol, and relationship observations are promoted together and exposed through MCP relationship queries; real analyzer output and AI-context retrieval remain to be validated. The real APK project run now persists functions, symbols, calls, and references through the current provider; MCP lookup retrieved stored functions and relationships, and an isolated PostgreSQL integration confirms complete promotion with zero pending rows. Selected-function explanations now receive bounded call edges and field/string references from the exact persisted function key, scoped to the same project, artifact, analysis run, and provider; a route regression verifies the context reaches the model input. Selected DEX member rewrites now resolve persisted method identities and supply bounded direct callers and callees from that same run; a focused route regression verified the selected method context reaches the rewrite model.
workstreams.remaining: Validate real APK explanation and rewrite retrieval with a configured model; validate identity consistency across providers and formats and over long project histories.
workstreams.basis: Project-scoped observations, symbols, relationships, drafts, and review records ground AI context. Common native virtual-address spellings now canonicalize across Ghidra, Glaurung, and Oxidizer for same-artifact function identity; bounded same-binary, completed-run lookups bring accepted cross-provider names into rewrite, explanation, and MCP dossier contexts for selected units with canonical-key or normalized native-identity matches, exact input-hash checks, and review-receipt verification. Durable function-pair records now preserve exact artifact hashes, analysis tasks, provider versions, function identities, bounded instruction/CFG snapshots, and append-only reviews; accepted pair names enter explanation context only when both the selected function identity and artifact hash match, with score and review provenance, and never auto-rename maintained source. Ghidra/Kuna lookalike context now retains the producing provider, analysis task, artifact identity and hash, normalized architecture, native function identity, and similarity score; opening an older match resolves its exact completed run only within the active project artifact selection. Fission, Ghidra, and Kuna same-function native reconstructions can now enter selected-unit rewrite context only when the input artifact hash, canonical address identity, completed provider run, and saved output hash all match; each is labeled provisional provider evidence. Recurse VTIL-style lift artifacts persist exact input/output hashes, provider revision, native function identity, and optimizer counters; rewrite context reads a same-function lift only from a completed run with exact input, identity, run-path, and output-hash checks, while labeling the lift as provisional structural evidence. Legacy native address aliases remain a fallback and are labeled separately because they can denote thunks. MCP provider outputs also require exact input and saved-output hashes; accepted project-memory lookup is bounded to 100 candidate provider observations and reports possible truncation. Exact-address ReIPA pseudocode alternatives for matched Swift/Objective-C methods enter rewrite context and MCP dossiers only after same-run provenance checks. Ghidra functions persist bounded basic-block/edge/entry/exit metrics and a bounded basic-block graph for the visualizer. Control-flow-flattening recovery now persists in function observation attributes and is available to the visualizer, rewrite/explanation, and MCP dossier as confidence-labeled structural evidence; it does not establish identity or behavior. Opt-in BcfClean and CffDeflatten pseudocode enters rewrite context only after the pinned provider version, same-artifact hash, exact address, saved-output hash, and successful emulation audit all match. The MCP code dossier now recomputes maintained-source and saved-draft hashes before exposing their code or validator results; Python bytecode units now retain hashes for both reconstructed source and disassembly, and the visualizer, MCP dossier, and module-level rewrite context verify those hashes; module-wide bytecode evidence is withheld from selected-function context unless a unique same-module code-object name match exists; maintained code also requires an accepted receipt matching the exact source bytes. Rewrite context now reads accepted symbols from immutable receipt snapshots and rehashes maintained callee source before using it. The visualizer and Ghidra export use the accepted receipt’s same symbol snapshot for historical rename names, lineage, and address annotations. Broader identity coverage and fixture validation remain open. PyInstaller bytecode children now persist as task-scoped derived artifacts with database code-unit records linking each module to the executable hash, archive member, extractor revision, and bytecode hash; up to four selected modules gain hash-verified pycdc source provenance, while remaining modules retain bytecode evidence for later review. PyInstaller selection now queries prior project observations using the exact executable hash and stable module code-unit key, so repeated runs continue through pending modules instead of restarting the same four-module batch. Scope-safe rename proposals are persisted as proposal-only attempts with the exact editable source and hash, accepted project-symbol context and hash, provider/model, and mappings; applied attempts link to that proposal and verify selected mappings against it. Attempt history displays and reloads saved proposals only after the current source hash and provider match. Prior proposals enter later AI prompts as unreviewed hints, never accepted evidence. TypeScript type-check, targeted ESLint, and Python AST parsing pass; runtime workflow and fixture evidence remain pending. The univdreams module observation stores the source and compile-back artifact paths, exact input/source/output hashes, pinned provider revision, and byte-identity verdict in the project database; the visualizer reads the persisted verdict rather than inferring it. Maintained Universal Dreams source validation now stores the compiler output as a source-and-output-hash-addressed artifact under the exact analysis run; the immutable review record carries that artifact path, output hash, source hash, and pinned compiler method. A maintained debug-ELF .ud module compiled back byte-identically after the narrow PLT-overlap backport, and the persisted artifact hash was independently checked; other format and behavior fixtures remain open. The REA Evidence v2 importer caps uploads at 8 MiB and 1,000 records, validates strict record shapes, profile and semantic hashes, record order and derived bundle manifests, then stores complete records with project-scoped idempotency. Only one exact project artifact SHA-256 match creates a link; unmatched or ambiguous records stay unbound. Up to twelve records for that exact artifact enter rewrite context as external untrusted data with their provider, confidence, authority, and limitations. Residual-unknown revision histories are explicitly unsupported and rejected rather than dropped; a searchable evidence review and explanation/MCP retrieval remain open.

workstreams.name: Major-language and format decompilation fluency
workstreams.summary: Useful Java, Android, .NET, Python, WebAssembly, native, and additional format paths exist at different maturity levels. A full run of the patched isolated Androguard analyzer against the stored 6.79 MB Cross Stitch Joy APK completed all 11,939 classes and all 33,401 implemented methods; it reported zero Unicode character-boundary panics and used no simple-output class fallbacks. This validates one APK and decompiler revision only, not broad Java or Kotlin fidelity.
workstreams.remaining: Major languages need idiomatic source recovery, broader project-level coverage, and versioned validation; several formats remain alternate views or early experiments.
workstreams.basis: Several useful Java, .NET, Android, Python, WebAssembly, and native paths exist, and matched arm64 Mach-O methods can now show early ReIPA C-like pseudocode beside Ghidra output; optional Glaurung and Kuna providers add bounded native C-like pseudocode, with Kuna also saving assembly and selected graph edges. Kuna's analyzer has built and completed an end-to-end system-ELF smoke run. Reko 0.12.5 now also passes an isolated runtime smoke on a generated PE, returning two address-keyed function artifacts with exact hashes. These native alternates still need representative fixture comparison and fidelity validation. Many languages remain navigation-only, early, or represented by generic pseudocode. The new isolated Arlecchino provider builds from its audited upstream revision, combines Vineflower, CFR, and JADX per class using compiler-error ranking, and stores canonical rename provenance, round-trip coverage, and hash-attributed output. Runtime and fixture fidelity remain unverified, so this adds a limited early JVM capability only. The pycdc provider stores a hash-attributed recovered Python source artifact and bounded bytecode disassembly, both linked to Python source units and verified by the visualizer. Selected-function context can include an exact-run code-object section when one matching name exists in the module, while ambiguous matches are omitted; module context retains the bounded full listing. A bounded isolated PyInstaller extractor now sends recovered `.pyc` members through that provider and preserves executable, archive-member, bytecode, and source hashes; only image-build and type-check evidence exist so far, so execution and source fidelity remain unvalidated. The ILSpy provider now applies a pinned NoFuserEx static ConfuserEx cleanup subset before decompilation, stores transformed assemblies separately with exact input/output hashes and pass provenance, and labels the output as intermediate; the image builds, while fixture-backed fidelity remains open. The webcrack analyzer also recovers embedded JavaScript/TypeScript from bounded local version 3 source maps, storing exact map and content provenance; maps are optional build evidence and may be stale, so broad TypeScript bundle reconstruction remains open. The isolated ILSpy analyzer now emits bounded, syntax-parsed Visual Basic-shaped translations from its C# reconstruction with exact source/output hashes and pinned CodeConverter provenance; this is an early bridge only, not recovered original VB, and fixture compilation and behavior checks remain open. A constrained CRuby 3.4.11 provider recognizes YARB ISeq artifacts and stores bounded raw disassembly plus a hash-verified structured sequence/opcode tree with locals, parameters, catch entries, opcode operands, and an early label-derived CFG. A bounded BSD-2-Clause Ruby 2.7-focused adapter now creates an experimental source candidate as a separate artifact when it passes CRuby 3.4.11 syntax parsing; the upstream is version-mismatched, so syntax acceptance does not establish behavior or fidelity. Vineflower now integrates the pinned Apache-2.0 Java Deobfuscator static Allatori flow pass for bounded JARs and stores a separate transformed artifact plus alternate sources when supported patterns are found; target code is not run, and behavior/fidelity comparison remains open. The pinned analyzer image now builds with the Allatori pass; provider runtime and fixture-backed fidelity remain open. A pinned isolated univdreams provider adds a low-level editable `.ud` view and compile-back evidence for supported ELF, PE, NE, thin Mach-O, WASM, and 6502 raw inputs. REAmon now byte-identically round-trips a minimal WASM module, small synthetic static ELF, optimized dynamic ELF, and debug dynamic ELF after a narrow PLT-overlap backport; maintained debug-ELF source validation also compiled and persisted the hash-verified binary. These small synthetic cases do not establish broad format coverage, behavior, or idiomatic source recovery. The pinned GPL-2.0-only Miasm adapter adds a provisional native deobfuscation view for supported PE/ELF architectures; x86-64 and AArch64 ELF plus two-function synthetic PE DLL export API smokes pass; broader architecture and fixture-backed fidelity remain open, and it does not produce original-language source.

workstreams.name: Maintainable editing, review, and export
workstreams.summary: Hash-bound drafts and immutable review receipts preserve lineage, with syntax validation, an early Java rebuild, and language-specific rename workflows now extending to C/C++ local bindings. Kotlin functions are now outlined and can be rewritten one at a time with grammar-aware member signature validation; focused isolated Docker coverage passes. DEX member rewrites now fetch direct callers/callees through the selected method observation keys instead of filtering a bounded run-wide edge prefix; focused route coverage verifies direct-callee source reaches rewrite context. The project function queue creates independently reviewable per-file drafts and keeps cross-file results separate; it does not auto-accept edits. Current source validation now uses the installed GCC/G++ compiler with `-fsyntax-only` for C/C++ maintained source; isolated Docker coverage confirms valid source passes and malformed source fails, with exact source hashes recorded. The authenticated endpoint was exercised on the rebuilt LAN agent: GCC 14.2.0 and G++ 14.2.0 accepted valid samples, rejected malformed samples, and returned matching SHA-256 values. Bounded project-level C# builds now compile up to 32 review-accepted files from one completed run together with Roslyn without executing the result; a PASSED or FAILED receipt records the exact artifact, run, source hashes, accepted review IDs, compiler version, and output assembly hash in project observations. The visualizer exposes the run-level action. Docker checks pass for cross-file symbol resolution, compiler rejection, stale hashes, receipt persistence routing, and the UI result state. Saved build receipts now reload from project observations only while the active completed run has the same complete accepted C# file set, review IDs, paths, and source hashes; edits or newly accepted files invalidate stale receipts. The UI restores the verified receipt after reload and guards against an earlier lookup overwriting a newly started build. Focused Docker coverage passes 9 route/component tests, Docker type-check passes, and targeted ESLint passes. The maintained-source ZIP now includes a whitelisted C# project build receipt only when the shared verifier confirms the complete accepted source set, review identities, and hashes still match; PASSED and FAILED validations remain distinguishable, while compiler diagnostic text and the compiled binary are not exported. Docker tests cover current receipt inclusion and stale-set omission.
workstreams.remaining: Exercise receipt retrieval and source export on a database-backed project; validate projects with external package references and target-specific build flags; broaden project builds and fixture-backed behavior checks to more languages and target formats.
workstreams.basis: Hash-bound drafts and review receipts preserve exact source lineage. New accepted reviews snapshot the exact source and symbol index; the visualizer can restore a verified prior source into a new review using that revision's saved rename context. Accepted-source promotion rejects failed or unavailable validation and prevents a previously accepted language-specific syntax check from silently downgrading to generic Tree-sitter evidence. An initial JVM rebuild path compiles one receipt-verified accepted Java class against the original JAR in the isolated JDK analyzer, patches matching class entries into a separate unsigned derived JAR, removes stale nested class files, and records the input/source/output hashes and compiler version in project observations. This is single-class build evidence only: signed and multi-release JARs, external dependency classpaths, cross-file builds, and runtime/fixture validation remain open. Syntax-aware edits cover selected languages, with reproducible export; the visualizer now exposes hash-pinned Phpactor LSP local-variable and parameter renames for PHP, validates rewritten source with PHP lint, and records the rename engine, mappings, and hashes in the existing reviewable attempt flow. A new C/C++ clangd adapter identifies same-file local variables and parameters, rejects unsupported macro/conditional/template forms and existing identifier collisions, checks edits against clangd's exact reference set, and stores the resulting mappings and hashes through the same attempt flow. The agent image builds and seven targeted synthetic C/C++ integration checks pass for grammar loading, local and parameter discovery, hash-bound semantic edits, stale-source and collision rejection, macro/template exclusions, and GCC/G++ syntax-check acceptance and rejection. Representative projects, complete reference coverage, and behavioral equivalence remain unvalidated. Broad language coverage and project-level edits remain limited. Saved rename proposals can be reviewed after reload and restored into the editor only when their source hash and provider still match; applying them remains a separate reviewed action. The proposal stage is explicitly marked unvalidated, and the resulting scope-aware transformation keeps its syntax/binding validation record and proposal lineage. Type-check and targeted lint pass; runtime rename fixtures remain open. Universal Dreams `.ud` edits now pass the pinned verify-and-compile step before acceptance, with compiled bytes stored under run evidence and the exact source/output hashes and path written into the immutable review receipt. The isolated container build, webapp type-check, and one synthetic WASM runtime validation pass; format and behavior fixture coverage remain open. Kotlin member editing now recognizes Kotlin-specific function names and function-body nodes for source outlines and member-scoped rewrites; the focused isolated Docker suite passes 26 cases, including exact outline ranges and a complete member rewrite validated by Tree-sitter and signature checks. This is editing support for existing Kotlin source, not Kotlin bytecode decompilation or behavior proof. The new C# project build validates only bounded accepted source files from one completed analysis run, uses the container platform references, emits an in-memory library, and never executes it. The project observation receipt is keyed to the exact normalized file-path/source-hash set and retains each accepted review ID. Compiler results distinguish successful and failed builds; unavailable compilers and stale sources do not create success receipts. Focused Docker checks pass, but authenticated LAN/browser and real project database acceptance remain pending. Receipt retrieval now revalidates the entire bounded accepted C# set for the selected active run, including newly added files, against immutable review hashes and the stored aggregate hash before showing build evidence; focused unit tests cover stale edits and new accepted files, while live database-backed acceptance remains open. Source-bundle export and receipt reload use one shared validator for stored build evidence. The archive manifest records only current, bounded compile metadata and per-file lineage; stale receipts are omitted and the compiled output is identified by hash without being included. The ZIP export tests also confirm failed compiler results remain evidence without exporting diagnostics.

workstreams.name: Fixture-backed validation and fidelity evidence
workstreams.summary: Provider smoke checks and structural validators provide early evidence; an isolated, stripped Lua 5.4 bytecode fixture now decompiles, parses with the matching compiler, and preserves the fixture observed runtime output.
workstreams.remaining: Build a broad, versioned fixture suite for clean, optimized, stripped, and obfuscated inputs and compare recovered behavior and fidelity.
workstreams.basis: Provider smoke checks and structural validators exist, but broad versioned clean, optimized, stripped, and obfuscated fixture comparisons are still missing. On 2026-10-26, a reproducible Docker fixture compiles a Lua 5.4 source sample with debug data stripped, decompiles it through the pinned unluac-rs worker, parses the recovered output with luac5.4, and confirms original and reconstructed output match. The test runs as UID/GID 10001 with no network, read-only root, 512 MiB memory, 64 processes, and dropped capabilities. This is one controlled fixture, not broad fidelity evidence.

workstreams.name: Security, reliability, and production operations
workstreams.summary: Project-scoped execution workers cover the four arbitrary-code tools, and the ticket-scoped terminal path is wired into the normal REAmon lifecycle. The dedicated language/compiler image builds and passes a constrained no-network runtime smoke; 36 focused broker worker tests pass. The restart-recovery path is deployed and passed a live isolated orphan-cleanup probe; end-to-end job flows and other worker controls remain open. The broker now closes interactive terminal sessions after 30 minutes idle by default and imposes a configurable hard session cap no greater than 115 minutes, below the signed graph-context lifetime; focused Docker tests verify both deadlines force worker/network cleanup. The broker image rebuild and 36 project-worker tests pass, including startup orphan-cleanup safety checks. On broker startup, REAmon now reaps labelled project-worker containers and networks before accepting work only when the Docker API confirms a single configured broker; multiple-broker or unavailable-inventory states skip destructive cleanup. The focused Docker worker suite passes 41 tests, including client-disconnect cancellation, cancellation during Docker create calls, and cleanup. That broker image is deployed healthy on the local PC; startup cleanup reported zero orphaned workers and networks. On 2026-10-26, kali_shell, execute_code, proxy_brain, and execute_playwright were made asynchronous end-to-end at the MCP boundary. Their cancellable broker client closes its TCP connection when the agent task is cancelled; the broker treats disconnect as a cancellation signal and removes the disposable worker. The focused MCP execution/capture Docker suite passed 51 tests and the broker worker Docker suite passed 42 tests, including socket cancellation and Docker Desktop bind-path coverage. Live deployment revealed and fixed three worker-launch mismatches: the broker and agent had different workspace mounts, the pentest worker tag did not match the built Kali image, and nested Docker Desktop bind mounts needed the daemon host path instead of its temporary WSL shim path. After rebuilding/recreating the broker and restarting Kali with no active sessions, jobs, or workers, a valid agent-signed direct call to the deployed async kali_shell function started a real sleep worker. Cancelling its task propagated through the broker socket; the worker container and network were removed, and the temporary project workspace was cleaned. FastMCP 3.2.4 registered all four tools as async. A live authenticated agent /kali/exec cancellation sends notifications/cancelled and removes the worker plus network. The notification shim has a focused Docker regression test (1 passed). Live /workspace/jobs and /sessions reads return 200 with master auth and 401 with scanner or missing auth; browser-level cancellation acceptance remains open.
workstreams.remaining: Verify browser-level cancellation end to end; complete browser-to-agent-to-broker source and terminal acceptance; coordinate multi-replica admission; add disk and destination-aware egress quotas; complete independent capacity review and release backup/restore drills.
workstreams.basis: Current source coverage includes five validated security findings with partial mitigations, master-only sensitive routes, signed scanner project scope, and non-terminal arbitrary-code execution for kali_shell, execute_code, proxy_brain, and execute_playwright. All four paths verify a short-lived signed agent context, run as host UID/GID 65534 in user, mount, and PID namespaces, and expose only the selected project at /workspace. The project root is read-only to the sandbox identity; only project `/tmp` scratch at `.reamon-tmp` and `tool-outputs` are writable, and the trusted agent rejects symlinked project roots/output directories before execution. Scratch persists between commands and files older than 24 hours are pruned. `/var/tmp`, `/dev/shm`, and `/opt/output` are private per-run mounts. Generated-file persistence canonicalizes the source under scratch and moves it into a unique project output path without a second full-size copy. Compiled C/C++ binaries run from scratch. Focused Docker suites pass 46 MCP execution/capture/Playwright tests plus 5 subtests and 15 agent identity/generated-file tests. Runtime smokes confirm read-only project roots, writable scratch/output, same-mount generated-file transfer, compiled C output, and sibling workspace/scratch/process isolation. At the initial broker rollout, Chromium launch, the deployed agent rebuild, deployed worker routing, shared broker ownership, and complete LAN validation remained open. The shared controller and root filesystem still serve multiple projects, so the Kali finding is not closed. Earlier focused CI run 40247230850 passed all five jobs on commit `baa5634a`, but CI success does not certify release readiness. Each non-terminal arbitrary-code child is now launched through the pinned image utility `/usr/bin/prlimit` with `RLIMIT_NOFILE=256` and `RLIMIT_CORE=0`; a focused Docker test and live Kali image probe confirmed inherited limits. These per-process controls reduce file-descriptor exhaustion and prevent core dumps but do not replace per-worker CPU, memory, disk, network, or idle-lifetime limits. The interactive PTY launcher now applies the same nofile and core-dump limits before entering its user/mount namespace; the terminal, arbitrary-execution, capture, and Playwright Docker suites pass together (54 tests plus 9 subtests). The ticket-bound interactive terminal now enters a PID namespace with a private `/proc`; focused Docker tests pass 7 tests plus 4 subtests, and a live Kali smoke showed the session shell at PID 1 with only its own namespace processes visible. The Docker broker no longer permits container creation when an enabled running-container cap cannot be verified. Its plumbing regression confirms the request is rejected without reaching the Docker API; Docker image suites pass 18 plumbing checks, 13 ownership checks, and 57 policy checks, including concurrent-create serialization under the cap. Broker-managed workers route kali_shell, execute_code, execute_playwright, and proxy_brain through a scanner-key-protected endpoint that revalidates signed context and tool scope, fails closed when capacity cannot be verified, and creates disposable containers with resource limits, read-only roots, project-only mounts, capped output, and per-run networks. The broker image builds. Thirteen focused worker tests, 14 MCP execution tests, and 27 capture-routing tests pass in Docker. A live Docker Engine smoke verified the immutable Kali image digest, project-only mount, read-only root, writable project scratch, independent stdout/stderr, and container/network cleanup. The local agent, Kali, and broker images were rebuilt from the pushed source and report healthy. A valid agent-signed broker request completed in a disposable worker with exit code 0, and worker/container network cleanup succeeded. Chromium launched in the active Kali image. At that rollout checkpoint, full dispatch through the MCP client/webapp, terminal workers, disk/idle/network quotas, tenant-scoped broker ownership, generated-file transfer, and upgrade/backup/restore validation remained open. On 2026-10-26 the rebuilt active Kali image passed `python3 -m pip check` with no broken requirements; `requests` 2.34.2, `urllib3` 2.8.0, and OpenTelemetry API 1.37.0 remain in the MCP environment. GraphQL-Cop, SSTImap, and AD tools run from isolated virtual environments; live command smokes passed for BloodHound, Certipy, BloodyAD, bhgraph, gMSADumper, GraphQL-Cop, and SSTImap. The `redamon-kali` service was recreated from this image and is healthy. Full MCP client/webapp routing, terminal workers, tenant-scoped broker ownership, egress and storage quotas, cancellation, and restart recovery remain open. The broker now hashes verified project IDs into stable SHA-256 Docker labels and counts only active workers carrying both the project-worker and matching project-scope labels. Under the broker admission lock, it enforces a configurable per-project ceiling (default two, never above the global ceiling of four) and fails closed if Docker cannot return a valid project count. Docker tests verify the hash-only label, filtered counts, denial at the per-project limit with global capacity remaining, and fail-closed behavior. Focused Docker suites pass 16 worker tests, 13 ownership checks, 18 plumbing checks, and 57 policy checks; Compose config validates. The rebuilt active broker is healthy and reports limits 4/2. Multi-replica admission coordination and worker disk, egress, and lifetime quotas remain open. Project workers now carry the dedicated `reamon.project-worker` and hashed project-scope labels, not the generic `redamon.broker-owned` label. The generic Docker API proxy rejects inspect, exec, attach, and other owned-container operations when it encounters a legacy dual-labeled project worker. Host capacity counts generic containers and project workers through separate fail-closed Docker queries. One shared admission lock serializes container creation through both the generic Docker API and signed worker API, preventing either path from bypassing the configured 48-container host cap on this broker process. Docker regression suites pass 18 worker tests, 17 ownership checks, 21 plumbing checks, and 57 policy checks. The rebuilt active broker is healthy with host cap 48 and worker caps 4/2. A live agent-signed `kali_shell` dispatch through the broker returned exit code 0, emitted the expected smoke marker, and left zero active project workers. Multi-replica coordination and LAN end-to-end verification remain open. Generic Docker container ownership is now separated from signed project workers, but the generic Docker proxy still forwards network API operations; scoping project-worker network lifecycle operations remains an open isolation gate. The restricted Docker proxy now denies all network API paths and network-bearing `/events` and `/system/df` endpoints, preventing project-worker network discovery and lifecycle changes through the generic socket. Generic container creation also rejects a `NetworkMode` beginning with the private `reamon-w-` prefix. Docker tests cover network list/inspect/create/connect/disconnect/delete/prune, event and disk-usage metadata, and private network attachment attempts. Focused Docker suites pass 19 worker tests, 17 ownership checks, 30 plumbing checks, and 58 policy checks. The rebuilt active broker is healthy with host cap 48 and worker limits 4/2. A live signed shell smoke succeeded with exit code 0 and confirmed zero active workers and zero host-cap usage afterward. Egress policy for intended scan traffic remains a separate quota/control gap. On 2026-10-26, Metasploit session-open events began recording agent user, project, and chat IDs in the session manager. Webapp session list/interact/kill routes now require strict ownership of the selected project; the agent forwards project scope and the session sidecar filters lists and verifies ownership before controls. Legacy sessions without metadata fail closed; project-scoped responses omit globally shared jobs. Switching projects clears previously loaded session rows. Focused Docker tests passed 19 Python cases across the ownership helpers and authenticated handler; 10 agent proxy tests, 10 webapp route/hook tests, TypeScript type-check, and Python compilation passed. Persistence across a session-service restart and LAN deployment remain unverified. In persistent mode the agent now refuses startup if PostgreSQL checkpoint initialization is unavailable, closes any partial pool, and does not silently switch to volatile MemorySaver; explicitly disabled mode retains the in-memory option. Four isolated Docker startup and shutdown tests pass, including checkpoint-pool cleanup. Live deployment recovery across an agent restart remains to be exercised. Session ownership metadata remains process-local because restarting Metasploit terminates the sessions it owns; no persistent historical session ledger is provided. A live PostgreSQL probe wrote a unique checkpoint, closed its first connection pool, recovered the state through a new pool, and deleted the probe thread; full agent restart recovery remains to be exercised. Checkpointer lifecycle regression tests confirm both the module-level saver and helper configuration switch away from a closed or stale saver on shutdown and when persistent mode is explicitly disabled; the focused Docker test file passes all four cases. The ticket-authenticated terminal proxy now sends only a five-minute agent-signed context to a dedicated broker endpoint. The broker checks the nested graph context and identity consistency, applies existing host/global/project admission limits, creates a capped per-session PTY container with project-only read-only workspace plus writable scratch/output, and removes it with its private network on disconnect. The trusted agent endpoint is attached to that session network only for signed graph calls. Source compilation and diff whitespace checks passed; Docker integration and live deployment acceptance have not yet run. The ticket-authenticated terminal proxy sends a five-minute agent-signed context containing a nested graph-only scope. The shared signed-context implementation now preserves this nested field identically across agent, recon, and capture-proxy copies. Focused Docker runs passed 11 agent identity/resolver tests, 27 broker worker tests, and 7 cross-copy context tests. A Docker Engine PTY smoke executed a shell command in a temporary project worker, returned output, and verified both container and network removal. That smoke patched scope verification, so the end-to-end agent/browser path and deployment remain unverified. On 2026-10-26, the normal lifecycle was corrected to build the dedicated REAmon project-worker image and start the filtered broker, with the agent and broker sharing the same workspace bind. Compose configuration validates with both profiles; the broker and worker images build, and the focused broker worker suite passes all 30 cases. A constrained no-network worker smoke ran Python, C, Java, Go, Node/TypeScript, Ruby, Perl, Rust, and .NET SDK 10.0.402 as UID/GID 65534 with a read-only root, dropped capabilities, and writable /tmp. The worker sets HOME and DOTNET_CLI_HOME under /tmp so compilers can write caches under the same project-scoped mount. The actual browser/agent path and LAN services were not restarted or verified; multi-replica admission, storage/egress/lifetime quotas, cancellation/restart cleanup, independent capacity review, and backup/restore drills remain release gates. Interactive terminal worker relays now enforce both idle and hard lifetime deadlines, clamp the hard cap beneath the signed graph context, close the browser-facing stream, and remove the disposable container/network in the normal cleanup path. Docker tests exercise idle timeout and absolute lifetime expiry; live LAN behavior remains unverified. A Docker broker startup reaper now lists broker, project-worker, and worker-network inventories before mutation; it only removes old worker resources when exactly one configured broker is visible, skips cleanup when more than one is present or inventory fails, and removes containers before their labelled networks. Focused Docker tests verify these cases and a fresh broker-image build passes. Live restart recovery remains unverified.
